note: Claim records for fascism and Nazism. status: drafted = written with sources linked; verified = an independent check confirmed the source supports the claim; reviewed = a named human expert signed off. conf rates the core claim of each record (that the event happened as described). Where a death toll or figure is disputed, the text gives the range and who made each estimate. Disputed numbers are never a reason to doubt that the crimes happened: Holocaust denial and minimization are not presented as a side. Graphic material is described only as far as history requires.

events.text: Benito Mussolini, editor of the Italian Socialist Party’s newspaper Avanti!, breaks with the party by calling for Italy to enter the First World War, starts his own paper and is expelled. This turn from socialism to nationalism set him on the road to Fascism.

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Benito Mussolini
World War I Document Archive (Brigham Young University Library), Benito Mussolini biography

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)

Softened; added his new paper; added a second source.

events.text: Mussolini founds the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento (Italian Combat Leagues) in Milan with about a hundred followers: war veterans and former shock troops, Futurist artists and ex-socialists. Its first program (June 1919) mixed nationalism with radical demands such as votes for women, an eight-hour day and a heavy tax on capital, most of which it dropped as it moved right in 1920–21. The name recalls the Roman fasces, a bundle of rods carried as a sign of authority, and gives us the word fascism.

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica, fasci di combattimento
AGI, Nicola Graziani, Cento anni fa nasceva il fascismo (23 March 2019)

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)

Corrected after this check: ‘Mostly war veterans and nationalists’ is not supported: the founders were about a hundred arditi (ex-shock troops), Futurists and ex-socialists. Britannica gives only ‘March 1919’, so added AGI for the exact date.

events.text: In Munich the German Workers’ Party, soon renamed the National Socialist German Workers’ Party (NSDAP), announces its 25-point program. It demands a Greater Germany, the overturning of the Versailles treaty, and citizenship only for people of ‘German blood’, stating outright that no Jew can belong to the nation. Its economic points include nationalizing trusts, profit-sharing in large firms and land reform; in 1928 Hitler stated that the land point was aimed only at Jewish speculators. Historians still argue over how seriously the economic points were meant (debate 3B).

sources.cite: German History in Documents and Images, NSDAP Party Program (1920)

events.text: Fascist squads converge on Rome. King Victor Emmanuel III declines to sign a martial-law decree that the army was ready to enforce, and appoints Mussolini prime minister of a coalition government. Historians debate why: fear of civil war, doubts about the army’s loyalty, and pressure from nationalists, business leaders and conservatives who saw Mussolini as a barrier to socialism are all cited. In form the appointment was legal; in practice it followed a threat of force and two years of squad violence against socialists, unions and local councils.

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica, March on Rome

events.text: Hitler and the Nazis try to seize power in Munich. Bavarian police stop the march with gunfire; four policemen and fourteen putschists die, and the putsch fails. Hitler is tried for treason. The court gives him the minimum sentence of five years and he is released after about nine months, during which he writes the first volume of Mein Kampf. The Nazis later honoured their dead from the putsch as martyrs.

sources.cite: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, Beer Hall Putsch (Munich Putsch)

events.text: A squad of Fascist militants led by Amerigo Dumini kidnaps and murders the Socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti after he denounces Fascist violence and fraud in the 1924 election. In the crisis that follows, opposition deputies walk out of parliament (the ‘Aventine secession’), but the King does not act. In January 1925 Mussolini tells parliament he takes responsibility for what happened and then builds an open dictatorship over the next two years.

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Matteotti Crisis
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Benito Mussolini

events.text: To crush armed resistance in Cyrenaica (eastern Libya) led by Omar al-Mukhtar, Italian forces deport 100,000–110,000 people, mostly women, children and the elderly, with their herds into desert concentration camps; the regime called it “pacification”. Historian Ali Abdullatif Ahmida says about two-thirds of them died; Italian historian Emilio Gentile counts about 50,000 deaths in the repression, and the exact toll is uncertain. Ahmida argues it was genocide; other historians call it an extreme colonial counter-insurgency.

events.text: President Paul von Hindenburg appoints Hitler chancellor at the head of a coalition with the conservative German National People’s Party, with Franz von Papen as vice chancellor. Nazis hold only three of the eleven cabinet posts, and Papen and his conservative allies believed they could control Hitler. Within months the Nazis had pushed them aside.

events.text: The Reichstag building burns. A young Dutch former Communist, Marinus van der Lubbe, is arrested at the scene and later executed. The Nazis claim it is the signal for a Communist uprising, and the next day an emergency decree suspends basic civil rights; the regime uses it to arrest thousands of Communists and other opponents. Whether van der Lubbe acted alone (Fritz Tobias, Hans Mommsen) or Nazis were involved (Benjamin Carter Hett, 2014) is still debated by historians.

events.text: The Reichstag passes the Enabling Act by 444 votes to 94, letting the government make laws without parliament. It reaches the two-thirds majority after all 81 Communist deputies and 26 Social Democrats are kept from their seats and armed SA and SS men fill the hall; the Catholic Centre Party and other non-socialist parties vote yes after promises from Hitler, and only the Social Democrats vote no.

events.text: The Nuremberg Laws strip German Jews of citizenship rights and ban marriage and sexual relations between Jews and other Germans. Nazi rules defined a Jew by ancestry, for example having three or more grandparents born into the Jewish community, whatever the person’s own faith.

events.text: Italy invades Ethiopia, a fellow member of the League of Nations, and takes Addis Ababa on 5 May 1936; League sanctions fail. Italian forces use chemical weapons, chiefly mustard gas dropped and sprayed from aircraft, in breach of the 1925 Geneva Protocol. Emperor Haile Selassie appeals to the League in person in June 1936; Ethiopian fighters (the Arbegnoch, or patriots) keep up resistance until British and Ethiopian forces drive Italy out in 1941. The war was popular in Italy, where the regime presented it as winning a place in the sun and avenging the defeat at Adwa (1896). Italy officially admitted using gas only in the mid-1990s.

events.text: A secret Japanese army unit in Manchuria carries out lethal human experiments from 1933; officially set up in 1936 and later known as Unit 731, it also developed biological weapons. Specialists widely accept that about 3,000 prisoners were killed at its Pingfang base near Harbin.

events.text: Army officers including Francisco Franco rise against Spain’s elected Popular Front government, starting the Spanish Civil War. The rebels said they were acting to stop disorder, attacks on the Catholic Church and a feared revolution, pointing to the murder of the monarchist leader José Calvo Sotelo by Republican police and militants on 13 July. Defenders of the Republic answer that it was a lawful, elected government and that the coup itself set off the revolution and the war. Germany and Italy send troops, aircraft and tanks to the Nationalists; the Soviet Union supplies the Republic, and Britain and France adopt non-intervention.

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Spain: The Civil War
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Spanish Civil War (summary)

events.text: After a grenade attack on Viceroy Rodolfo Graziani by two young Eritreans, Italian soldiers, Fascist Blackshirt militia and Italian civilians kill residents across Addis Ababa for three days. Estimates of the dead range from about 3,000 (Italian historian Angelo Del Boca and British writer Anthony Mockler) to about 19,000 (Ian Campbell, 2017) and 30,000 (Ethiopian sources). In May 1937 Italian forces also shot the monks of the Debre Libanos monastery.

events.text: Aircraft of the German Condor Legion, joined by Italian planes, bomb the Basque town of Guernica (Gernika) on a market day, killing many civilians. The toll is disputed: the Basque government recorded 1,654 deaths in 1937 and historian Xabier Irujo argues for 2,000 or more, while Spanish air force general Jesús Salas put it at about 120, and many accounts give 120 to 300. Franco’s side claimed retreating Republicans had burned the town; Picasso’s painting made Guernica a worldwide symbol.

events.text: After capturing Nanjing on 13 December 1937, Japanese troops kill surrendered soldiers and civilians on a mass scale, with widespread sexual violence against women and girls, looting and arson. Estimates depend on the area, period and victims counted: China’s government gives 300,000 or more, the postwar Tokyo tribunal more than 100,000 (in its verdict on General Matsui), and Japanese historians from about 40,000 (Hata Ikuhiko) to 160,000–170,000 (Kasahara Tokushi). Foreign residents led by John Rabe ran a Safety Zone that sheltered over 200,000 civilians; denial of the massacre is not a scholarly side.

events.text: German troops enter Austria unopposed and large crowds welcome Hitler in Vienna; Germany annexes the country (the Anschluss). Violence against Austrian Jews, including forced public humiliation, beatings and looting, follows at once. A plebiscite in April 1938, held under heavy pressure and with Jews and opponents excluded, reports 99.7 percent approval. After 1945 Austria long described itself as Hitler’s ‘first victim’; in 1991 Chancellor Franz Vranitzky acknowledged that Austrians also shared responsibility for Nazi crimes.

sources.cite: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, German annexation of Austria (timeline)

events.text: Britain, France, Germany and Italy agree at Munich that Czechoslovakia must cede the Sudetenland to Germany; Czechoslovakia is not party to the decision, nor is the Soviet Union. British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain says it means ‘peace for our time’. Poland and Hungary also take Czechoslovak territory in the following weeks. Whether appeasement was a grave mistake or a rational way to buy time to rearm is still debated (debate F).

sources.cite: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, Munich Agreement (timeline)

events.text: Fascist Italy passes racial laws that expel Jews from schools, universities, the civil service and the armed forces and ban marriages between Jews and other Italians. Many Italian Jews had been Fascist party members, and the laws shocked them. Historians once tended to see the laws as Mussolini copying Hitler to please his ally (Renzo De Felice); later research, notably Michele Sarfatti’s, stresses the Fascist regime’s own racist and antisemitic motives, already visible in its colonial laws.

sources.cite: Simon Wiesenthal Center Annual, vol. 4, Refuge and Persecution in Italy, 1933–1945
USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, Italia (Italian edition)

events.text: Using the shooting of the German diplomat Ernst vom Rath in Paris by Herschel Grynszpan, a young Polish Jew whose family had just been expelled from Germany, as a pretext, the regime organizes a pogrom across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland. Propaganda presented it as spontaneous popular anger; in fact party and SA leaders, urged on by Goebbels, organized it. More than 1,400 synagogues are burned or destroyed, thousands of Jewish businesses are wrecked, at least 91 Jews are killed and hundreds more die after arrest or by suicide, and about 26,000–30,000 Jewish men are sent to concentration camps. The state then fines German Jews one billion Reichsmarks. Many historians now prefer the name ‘November pogrom’, because ‘Kristallnacht’ (night of broken glass) makes it sound as if only property was damaged.

sources.cite: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, Kristallnacht

events.text: Madrid falls on 28 March 1939 and Franco declares the war over on 1 April; Britannica puts the war’s dead at about 500,000. Killings behind the lines happened on both sides: about 50,000 in the Republican zone, mostly by militias in the first months, including about 6,800 clergy and the prisoners shot at Paracuellos in 1936; on the Nationalist side killing was ordered policy, with estimates from about 80,000 by 1943 (a conservative figure cited by Britannica) to about 150,000 (Paul Preston), and executions went on for years after 1939. About 450,000 Spaniards fled to France in early 1939.

events.text: Germany invades Poland, starting the Second World War in Europe; Britain and France declare war on 3 September. Under a secret protocol of the Nazi–Soviet Pact of 23 August 1939, the Soviet Union invades eastern Poland on 17 September, and the two powers divide the country.

sources.cite: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, German invasion of Poland (timeline)

events.text: Hitler secretly authorizes the murder of institutionalized disabled people, backdating the order to 1 September 1939. The regime called it ‘euthanasia’ (mercy killing), but the victims were not dying and did not consent; they were killed because the regime judged their lives ‘unworthy of life’. T4’s own count is 70,273 people gassed in six centers by August 1941. After public protests, including a sermon by Bishop Clemens August von Galen of Münster in August 1941, the gassing in those centers was stopped, but killing by starvation, drugs and shooting went on; historians estimate about 250,000 victims across all phases.

sources.cite: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, Nazi Euthanasia Program

events.text: The first Polish prisoners arrive at Auschwitz, a camp the SS set up that spring. Auschwitz grew into the largest killing site of the Holocaust, where about 1.1 million people were killed: about 1 million Jews, and also about 70,000–75,000 non-Jewish Poles, about 21,000 Roma and Sinti, about 15,000 Soviet prisoners of war and some 10,000–15,000 others.

sources.cite: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, Auschwitz

events.text: After France’s defeat, parliament votes 569 to 80 to give Marshal Philippe Pétain, the most admired French commander of the First World War, full powers, and the Vichy regime replaces the Republic. Pétain promised a ‘National Revolution’ under the motto ‘Work, Family, Fatherland’, and many French people, shocked by defeat, at first trusted him. In October 1940 Vichy issues, on its own initiative, a Statute on Jews excluding them from public service and many professions, extended in June 1941.

events.text: After the Axis invasion of Yugoslavia, Germany and Italy set up the Independent State of Croatia with Ante Pavelić and the Ustaše in power. Some Croats at first welcomed independence after two decades in a Serb-dominated kingdom; the Ustaše regime then persecuted and murdered Serbs, Jews and Roma, and also killed Croat and Muslim opponents, while also forcing many Serbs to convert to Catholicism.

SS and police units (Einsatzgruppen), with army support and local auxiliaries, begin mass shootings of Jews behind the front, and army orders such as the Commissar Order told troops to shoot Soviet political officers on capture.

events.text: At the Babi Yar (Babyn Yar) ravine outside Kyiv, SS and police units, guided by Einsatzgruppe C and helped by Ukrainian auxiliary police, shoot 33,771 Jews in two days, according to their own reports. In the months that followed Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, psychiatric patients and others were also killed there; Soviet investigators later estimated about 100,000 people were killed at the site. Soviet memorials long avoided saying that most victims were Jews.

Prisoners revolted at Treblinka in August 1943 and at Sobibor in October 1943; some hundreds escaped, and only a few dozen from each camp survived the war.

events.text: French police arrest about 13,000 Jews in Paris, about 4,000 of them children, and hold many in the Vélodrome d’Hiver before deportation to Auschwitz; very few survived. The police had planned to arrest about 27,000; many others escaped after warnings, some of them from police officers and neighbours. In 1995 President Jacques Chirac acknowledged the French state’s responsibility.

events.text: Hans Scholl, Sophie Scholl and Christoph Probst of the White Rose, a student resistance group in Munich that distributed anti-Nazi leaflets, are executed days after their arrest. Other German resistance came from Communists, Social Democrats and trade unionists, who filled the first camps in 1933, from church members, and from individuals such as Georg Elser, who tried to kill Hitler with a bomb in November 1939.

events.text: Jewish fighters of the Jewish Combat Organization (ŻOB), led by Mordechai Anielewicz, and the Jewish Military Union (ŻZW) resist the final deportations from the Warsaw ghetto for nearly a month, the largest Jewish uprising of the war. German forces burn the ghetto block by block; the SS commander Jürgen Stroop reported more than 56,000 Jews captured, and most survivors were deported to Treblinka and other camps.

events.text: Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg sets off a bomb at Hitler’s headquarters in East Prussia; Hitler survives, the coup fails, and the regime executes many of the conspirators and arrests thousands of suspects. events.text: The International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg tries 22 leading Nazis on four counts, including crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Nineteen are convicted, 12 of them sentenced to death, and three are acquitted. Critics then and since have called it victors’ justice: Allied conduct was not judged, and the Soviet prosecutors even charged Germany with the Katyn massacre of Polish officers, which Soviet forces had carried out. Defenders point to the mass of documentary evidence, the defense lawyers and the acquittals, and to the trial’s lasting role in international law.

events.text: The International Military Tribunal for the Far East tries Japanese wartime leaders; seven, including Tōjō Hideki, are hanged on 23 December 1948. The United States decided not to indict Emperor Hirohito; how much responsibility he bore is debated (Herbert Bix argues a great deal; others stress the military’s control). The Indian judge Radhabinod Pal dissented, voting to acquit all defendants: he accepted that atrocities such as those at Nanjing happened, but argued that the charge of aggressive war was retroactive law and that the Western powers were judging others for what they had done in their own empires. His dissent is still cited by Japanese nationalists and criticized by many historians.

sources.cite: National WWII Museum, Tokyo War Crimes Trial
Encyclopaedia Britannica, International Military Tribunal for the Far East

events.text: Ion Antonescu, Romania’s wartime dictator, is executed after a trial by a Romanian people’s tribunal for war crimes, including the murder of Jews. The tribunal sat under Soviet occupation and growing Communist control, which later critics used to question its fairness. In the 1990s some Romanian nationalists tried to rehabilitate Antonescu; in 2004 the international Wiesel Commission, set up by the Romanian state, confirmed his regime’s responsibility for the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Jews and Roma.

In 1995 its successor, National Alliance, formally renounced fascism. Brothers of Italy, founded in 2012 by former National Alliance members, describes itself as a conservative party; critics point to its roots in the MSI and to the tricolour flame it kept in its logo.

events.text: The historians’ dispute (Historikerstreit) breaks out in West Germany after Ernst Nolte suggests that Nazi crimes were in part a reaction to Bolshevik terror, which he called their precedent. Jürgen Habermas and most historians rejected his causal claim as relativizing the Holocaust; comparison of Nazi and Soviet crimes nonetheless became normal scholarship.

people.name: Benito Mussolini
people.text: Former socialist editor who founded Fascism in 1919, became prime minister in 1922 and dictator by 1925, and allied Italy with Nazi Germany. He was called Il Duce (‘the leader’, from the Latin dux), the title at the centre of a personality cult built by the regime; supporters at home and some admirers abroad praised him in the 1920s for restoring order, while opponents were beaten, jailed, exiled to remote islands or killed. Deposed in 1943, he was shot by partisans in April 1945.

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica

people.name: Adolf Hitler
people.text: Leader of the Nazi Party from 1921 and dictator of Germany from 1933 to 1945. After President Hindenburg died in August 1934 he merged the offices of chancellor and president and took the title Führer (‘leader’), to whom soldiers and officials swore personal oaths; the regime’s propaganda presented him as the nation’s saviour. He started the Second World War in Europe and drove the genocide of European Jews and other mass murders.

sources.cite: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, Adolf Hitler

people.name: Francisco Franco
people.text: General who led the Nationalist side in the Spanish Civil War with German and Italian help and ruled Spain as dictator from 1939 until his death, with the title Caudillo (‘leader’), which his regime used to present him as the saviour of Catholic Spain. Supporters credit him with keeping Spain out of the Second World War and with the economic growth of the 1960s; critics point to mass executions, prisons and labour camps, and decades of repression. Whether his regime was fascist or authoritarian-conservative is debated.

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica

people.name: Ion Antonescu
people.text: General who ruled Romania as dictator from 1940 to 1944 in alliance with Nazi Germany. His regime murdered hundreds of thousands of Jews, mainly in Bessarabia, Bukovina and Transnistria, and deported about 25,000 Roma to Transnistria, where at least 11,000 died; he was executed in 1946.

sources.cite: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, Romania

people.name: Ante Pavelić
people.text: Founder of the Ustaše movement and head of the Independent State of Croatia from 1941 to 1945, with the title Poglavnik (‘leader’). His regime murdered Serbs, Jews and Roma as well as Croat and Muslim opponents. He escaped in 1948 to Argentina through the ‘ratlines’, escape routes run with help from some Catholic clergy in Rome, and died in Madrid in 1959.

people.name: Tōjō Hideki
people.text: Army general and prime minister of Japan from October 1941 to July 1944, who led the country into war with the United States and Britain. He was convicted by the Tokyo tribunal and hanged in 1948. In 1978 he and other convicted leaders were enshrined at the Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo, so visits there by Japanese prime ministers draw protests from China and South Korea; visitors say they honour all of Japan’s war dead.

He supported the German-backed Salò Republic and was killed in Florence in April 1944 by a communist partisan unit; the killing was debated even within the Resistance.

people.name: Anne Frank

The helpers who hid the family, including Miep Gies, were later honoured for it.
